subject.title: Strange Service
subject.author: Ivor Gurney
subject.text:
Little did I dream, England, that you bore me

Under the Cotswold hills beside the water meadows,

To do you dreadful service, here, beyond your borders

And your enfolding seas.

  I was a dreamer ever, and bound to your dear service,

Meditating deep, I thought on your secret beauty,

As through a child's face one may see the clear spirit

Miraculously shining.


  Your hills not only hills, but friends of mine and kindly,

Your tiny knolls and orchards hidden beside the river

Muddy and strongly flowing, with shy and tiny streamlets

Safe in its bosom.

 
Now these are memories only, and your skies and rushy sky-pools

Fragile mirrors easily broken by moving airs ...

But deep in my heart for ever goes on your daily being,

And uses consecrate.



 
Think on me too, O Mother, who wrest my soul to serve you

In strange and fearful ways beyond your encircling waters;

None but you can know my heart, its tears and sacrifice;

None, but you, repay.

title: A Debt Nobody Worked Out How to Repay
standfirst: In November 1917 Ivor Gurney's first book demanded that England alone could know, and repay, the cost of his service. He had tried to enlist three years earlier and had broken down two years before that — evidence, his biographers now argue, of an illness the war did not cause and never fully explained.

sections.heading: A Bill Addressed Only to England
Two Pages, Two Very Different Prayers
sections.body:
Strange Service is not the book's opening poem — it is the seventh, on page 23 of a seventy-page collection — but it opens a short run of poems addressing England directly: Serenity, The Signaller's Vision, The Mother and To England—A Note all follow within the next five pages. Forty-four pages later, the book's very last poem, a sonnet called [England the Mother](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/63895/63895-h/63895-h.htm), closes on the same appeal: We have done our utmost, England, terrible / And dear taskmistress, darling Mother and stern. Gurney built his first book to open and close on the same address to the same feminised country.

Turn the page from Strange Service, though, and the tone breaks completely. Serenity, printed directly after it, abandons pleading almost entirely — seven lines built from one line repeated three times:

> Nor steel nor flame has any power on me,
> Save that its malice work the Almighty Will,
> Nor steel nor flame has any power on me;
> Through tempests of hell-fire I must go free
> And unafraid...

No Mother, no transaction, just a soldier declaring himself untouchable by anything short of providence. Two poems, two pages apart in the same short book, and they do not agree about what a soldier owes his war, or who he owes it to. The Mother-and-service voice of Strange Service — wrest my soul to serve you, uses consecrate — is not incidental vocabulary either: Gurney sang as a [chorister at Gloucester Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivor_Gurney) for six years before becoming an articled pupil to the cathedral organist, Herbert Brewer. The language of consecration was the first vocabulary he owned, well before he owned any other.

sections.heading: Hills That Had Already Done This Work Once
sections.body:
Your hills not only hills, but friends of mine and kindly is usually read as homesick decoration. It is not decoration. In 1913, two years before Gurney owned a uniform, his time at the Royal College of Music ended in a breakdown severe enough to send him home to Gloucestershire — his biographer Michael Hurd traced it to a student [unable in term-time to glimpse the restoring countryside](https://englishassociation.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/2.14.2.4-Publications-Bookmarks-First-World-War-Bookmarks-Ivor-Gurney-by-Ian-Brinton.pdf). He recovered at the Lock House in Framilode, and a small hill near it, together with Crickley Hill above Gloucester, became the places he returned to in his mind for the rest of his life. He described the Framilode hill himself, in a letter to Marion Scott written some time between that breakdown and the outbreak of war:

> a small hill not a mile away... gives one a view of the Forest of Dean, hills on the West, the whole broad Severn on the SW... Oh, what a place!

By the time Strange Service credited England's dreadful service with wresting his soul into shape, the hills it names as friends had already done exactly that work, once, on their own, with no war anywhere near them.

sections.heading: A Cure He Enlisted For
sections.body:
Gurney went looking for the army before there was any obligation to. He volunteered in August 1914, within weeks of the declaration of war, and was [turned down on the grounds of poor eyesight](https://warpoets.org.uk/worldwar1/poets-and-poetry/ivor-gurney/). He tried again in February 1915 and was accepted, as a private. His biographer Kate Kennedy argues that the enlistment itself was partly medicinal: he had already suffered a breakdown at music college, and had [enlisted to try to cure himself](https://press.princeton.edu/ideas/ivor-gurney-writing-in-lockdown-for-fifteen-years) of his neurasthenia, as he called it — the structure of army life, and its exhausting routines, briefly did what nothing else had.

Gurney used the same word himself, in a letter to Marion Scott written from the trenches near Laventie in the summer of 1916, with home plainly on his mind: But in the name of all the Pleiades what has a neurasthenic musician to do with all this? By the time he published Strange Service's demand for recognition of his tears and sacrifice, he had already diagnosed the underlying condition himself, more than a year earlier, in his own hand.

sections.heading: None, But You, Repay
sections.body:
The version of Gurney's story that circulated after his death supplied its own answer to the poem's demand, and got the underlying account wrong. According to the [Western Front Association's](https://www.westernfrontassociation.com/world-war-i-articles/ivor-gurney-composer-poet-soldier/) history of Gurney, the shell-shock narrative derives largely from his closest friend and champion, Marion Scott, who framed his final illness as war-caused in the accounts she gave after his death — even though he had clearly shown signs and symptoms of a bipolar disorder since his teens. Oxford's own war archive puts it just as plainly: it is [generally accepted now that his illness predates the War](https://war.web.ox.ac.uk/ivor-gurney).

By 1922 his family had him committed, first to Barnwood House near Gloucester, then to the City of London Mental Hospital at Dartford, where his identity narrowed to a file: patient no. 6420. His doctors treated his own biography as symptomatic rather than factual. The patient is said to be musical, one note records. The patient prays for death. He claims to have been assistant organist at Gloucester cathedral. He had been — for five years, under Herbert Brewer — before anyone thought to doubt him.

He died there in 1937, having spent his last fifteen years asking to be believed by people who no longer had reason to take his word for anything. Strange Service ends by telling England that none but you can know my heart, its tears and sacrifice; none, but you, repay. Neither England, nor the friends who explained his collapse using this poem's own vocabulary of service and sacrifice, ever really worked out what that debt was for.
